title: Web Crawler
oneLine: Drive fetching from a durable, prioritized, host-aware frontier; enforce robots and politeness, deduplicate URLs and content, and make every stage resumable.
opening: The core is a durable URL frontier, not just a pool of HTTP workers. Seed URLs enter a normalized seen-set and a prioritized frontier. A scheduler separates global priority from per-host queues so we respect robots.txt and politeness delays while keeping workers busy. Fetchers use cached DNS, deadlines, size/type limits, and conditional requests. Parsed pages are content-hashed to remove duplicates, persisted, and passed to an extractor that normalizes and filters new links before they re-enter the frontier. I would partition primarily by host/domain so one scheduler owns politeness for that host, checkpoint every stage, and track freshness, crawl budget, trap detection, and fetch outcomes.
ask: Is the goal search indexing, archival, monitoring, or a focused domain crawl?
How many pages, how fresh, and which content types/languages?
What legal/robots/politeness and per-site budget rules apply?
scale: Average fetch rate is target pages ÷ crawl interval; bandwidth usually dominates before CPU parsing.
Partition by host to serialize host-level politeness while running many hosts concurrently.
The seen set may reach billions of URLs; use durable partitioned storage plus Bloom filters as an optimization, not the only source of truth.

decisions.default: Front queues for priority/freshness and back queues per host for politeness.
decisions.why: A single FIFO cannot balance importance with per-site rate limits.
decisions.switch: Specialized crawls can use topic/domain-specific queues and explicit customer SLAs.

decisions.default: Hash by host/domain for scheduling ownership.
decisions.why: It centralizes robots and next-allowed-fetch state for each site.
decisions.switch: Very large hosts may require controlled subpartitioning with a shared token budget.

decisions.default: Fetch static HTML by default; send selected pages to a sandboxed browser-render queue.
decisions.why: Headless rendering is expensive and vulnerable to hostile scripts.
decisions.switch: Render all pages only for narrow, high-value domains where dynamic content is essential.

decisions.default: Adapt revisit interval from change frequency, importance, and HTTP cache headers.
decisions.why: Uniform recrawl wastes bandwidth on static pages and misses fast-changing ones.
decisions.switch: Event/webhook feeds can replace polling for cooperative sources.

deepDives.title: URL normalization
points: Canonicalize scheme/host, remove fragments, normalize default ports, and treat query rules carefully.
Respect canonical tags but do not trust them blindly.
Avoid collapsing distinct signed or order-sensitive URLs.

deepDives.title: Politeness and robots
points: Cache robots.txt with expiry and fail conservatively according to policy.
Maintain per-host next-fetch time and concurrent-connection limit.
Identify the crawler honestly and provide contact/takedown mechanisms.

deepDives.title: Trap defense
points: Cap URL length, path depth, calendar patterns, duplicate parameter combinations, and pages per host.
Detect near-duplicate content and infinite generated spaces.
Sandbox parsers/renderers and enforce byte/time/memory limits.

failures.response: Per-host budget, pattern detectors, depth/parameter caps, and operator quarantine.
Host queues and token budgets; fairness scheduler across domains.
Durable leases with visibility timeout, idempotent fetch records, checkpoints, and retry classes.
DNS cache with TTL, exponential backoff, circuit state per host, and conditional retries by status class.

questions.a: Conceptually discovery can look breadth-first, but production scheduling is priority- and politeness-driven. Important/fresh URLs and host budgets matter more than strict graph depth.
Hash normalized bytes for exact duplicates and use locality-sensitive fingerprints such as SimHash/MinHash for near duplicates. Keep canonical/source relationships for indexing.

questions.q: How do you guarantee each URL is fetched once?
questions.a: Usually you do not need a global exactly-once guarantee. Use at-least-once leases and idempotent storage; duplicate fetches are cheaper than distributed coordination over every URL.

questions.q: How do you scale one huge domain?
questions.a: Split paths across workers but keep a shared host-level rate budget and robots policy. A coordinator or distributed token bucket prevents aggregate politeness violations.

mistakes: Describing only worker threads and no frontier
Using Bloom filters as authoritative dedupe despite false positives
Rendering arbitrary JavaScript without sandbox/resource limits
seniorSignal: Focus on scheduling fairness, crawl budget, legal/politeness controls, resumability, and hostile-input isolation—not merely HTTP throughput.
implementation: Kafka/Pulsar partitions for durable frontier stages, with a host-aware scheduler
RocksDB/Cassandra seen set plus Bloom filters
Object storage for raw content; parser/index pipeline downstream
Playwright/Chromium workers in strict sandbox for selected dynamic pages
